planting.note: Divide and plant rhizomes shallowly in fall so roots establish before the spring bloom flush.

directions: Bred by M.D. Faith and registered in 2002, this Louisiana iris carries lightly ruffled blue-purple standards and darker blue-purple falls centered with a large golden-yellow signal edged in creamy white. It won the Mary Swords DeBaillon Medal in 2013, the top honor for Louisiana irises. Grow in consistently moist to boggy, humus-rich soil in full sun and divide every three to four years to keep clumps vigorous.

planting.note: Plant divisions in fall into damp, fertile soil for a strong midseason bloom the following spring.

directions: Hybridized by Patrick O'Connor of Metairie, Louisiana and registered in 2015, this striking cultivar bears deep red-orange standards edged in yellow, with falls that are red-orange on the upper half and veined red-orange over a yellow ground on the lower half around a yellow thumbprint signal. After years of accumulating honors it received the Mary Swords DeBaillon Medal in 2025. It performs best in sun to light shade with abundant moisture through the growing season.

planting.note: Set rhizomes just below the soil surface in fall for spring bloom.

directions: Patrick O'Connor named this pale blue Louisiana iris for Bywater, a historic New Orleans neighborhood near the Mississippi River, continuing his tradition of drawing cultivar names from the city's streets and districts. The soft, clear blue flowers show the open, flaring form typical of modern Louisiana iris breeding. Give it rich, moisture-retentive soil and full sun to bloom well.

planting.note: Fall division and planting lets clumps settle before spring flowering.

directions: Hybridized by Patrick O'Connor and named for Nottoway, the famous Louisiana River Road plantation house, this cultivar carries pure white blooms. It fits well among other white-flowered Louisiana irises in a bog garden or pond margin planting. Like other Louisiana iris, it thrives with constant moisture and rich organic soil.

planting.note: Divide and reset rhizomes in fall for best spring flowering.

directions: Patrick O'Connor named this red-flowered Louisiana iris for Highland Road, a well-known street in Baton Rouge. The saturated red blooms stand out well against the strappy, glossy foliage typical of the Iris x louisiana group. Grow in full sun with consistently wet to moist soil, as in a rain garden or pond edge.

planting.note: Plant divisions in fall into wet, fertile soil ahead of the spring bloom season.

directions: Hybridized by Patrick O'Connor, this red Louisiana iris takes its name from Storyville, the historic New Orleans district, part of his pattern of naming introductions for the city's neighborhoods and landmarks. The bold red color reads well in mass plantings along ponds and ditches. Provide full sun and steady moisture for best performance.

planting.note: Fall planting of divisions gives clumps time to root before spring bloom.

directions: Patrick O'Connor named this red Louisiana iris for New Orleans's historic Charity Hospital, continuing his habit of commemorating the city's landmarks in his introductions. It carries the large, ruffled, red flowers typical of contemporary Louisiana iris breeding. Grow in full sun with rich, moisture-retentive soil, as along a pond edge or low wet spot.

planting.note: Divide and plant in fall so roots are established before spring flowering.

directions: Hybridized by Patrick O'Connor and named for Monkey Hill, the famous artificial hill at the Audubon Zoo in New Orleans, this medium-height cultivar bears red flowers. Its moderate stature suits smaller water-garden plantings and mixed perennial borders where taller Louisiana iris would overwhelm the scene. Keep soil consistently moist to wet through the growing season.

planting.note: Plant divisions in fall; doubled-flower forms benefit from a sheltered spot out of strong wind.

directions: Bred by Lake Charles hybridizer Marvin Granger, this Louisiana iris is a yellow double-flowered form, following up on the blue doubles Granger first discovered breeding Louisiana iris in the mid-1950s. The multiplied petal segments give the bloom a fuller, rounder look than single-form cultivars. Grow in full sun with rich, constantly moist to wet soil.

planting.note: Plant divisions in fall; this late bloomer extends the Louisiana iris season into early summer.

directions: Hybridized by Marvin Granger of Lake Charles, Louisiana, this rose-pink Louisiana iris is noted for blooming very late in the season, extending color after most other cultivars have finished. It pairs well with later-blooming perennials around pond margins. Provide full sun and steadily moist to wet, fertile soil.

planting.note: Fall division and planting supports strong spring bloom.

directions: Bred by Marvin Granger, this Louisiana iris bears velvety deep purple flowers set off by contrasting white style arms. The dark, richly textured petals make it a strong accent plant among lighter-colored companions at a pond edge or bog garden. Grow in full sun with consistently wet, humus-rich soil.

planting.note: Plant divisions in fall into moist soil for spring bloom.

directions: Hybridized by Heather Pryor, one of the leading modern Louisiana iris breeders working with the Taylor/Nichols lines, this cultivar produces clear yellow flowers. It is counted among the notable yellow-flowered Louisiana iris introductions of recent decades. Grow in full sun to light shade with abundant, consistent moisture.

planting.note: Divide and replant clumps in early fall or early spring to re-establish before bloom.

directions: Bred by Dr. Currier McEwen, a pioneer of tetraploid Siberian iris breeding, this cultivar bears pure white flowers with the broader, fuller form McEwen's tetraploid introductions were known for. It is a good companion for blue- and purple-flowered Siberian iris selections in a mixed perennial bed. Grow in full sun to light shade with average to moist, well-drained garden soil.

planting.note: Replant divisions in early fall or early spring for best establishment.

directions: A companion introduction to 'Fourfold White' from tetraploid Siberian iris breeder Dr. Currier McEwen, this cultivar carries soft lavender flowers on the sturdy, well-branched stems typical of his tetraploid line. It combines easily with other pastel perennials in a border or alongside a pond. Grow in full sun to light shade in average to consistently moist soil.

planting.note: Divide congested clumps in early fall or early spring and replant promptly.

directions: Registered in 1992 by Dr. Currier McEwen, this Siberian iris was one of his later tetraploid introductions, developed as part of his decades-long program that produced around 100 Siberian iris cultivars. It grows well in average garden soil with regular moisture and performs reliably in full sun to light shade. Clumps increase steadily and benefit from division every three to four years.

planting.note: Divide and replant in early fall or early spring; avoid disturbing in hot weather.

directions: Registered in 1991 by Dr. Currier McEwen, this tetraploid Siberian iris bears lilac-toned flowers, part of a long run of McEwen introductions that broadened the color range and form of modern Siberian iris. It is well suited to perennial borders and pond-edge plantings where its grassy foliage provides structure after bloom. Grow in full sun to light shade with evenly moist, well-drained soil.

planting.note: Replant divisions in early fall or early spring; established clumps need little further care.

directions: Registered in 1991 by Dr. Currier McEwen, this white-flowered Siberian iris is named, like his related 'Harpswell Happiness', for Harpswell, Maine, where McEwen gardened and bred irises for decades. Its tall stems and clean white blooms make a strong focal point against darker-flowered Siberian iris nearby. Grow in full sun to light shade with consistently moist, fertile soil.

planting.note: Divide and replant in early fall or early spring for quickest re-establishment.

directions: Another of Dr. Currier McEwen's "Harpswell" series of tetraploid Siberian iris, named for his home town of Harpswell, Maine, alongside sister cultivars 'Harpswell Happiness' and 'Harpswell Snowburst'. McEwen's Harpswell introductions are prized for sturdy stems and vigorous, long-lived clumps. Grow in full sun to light shade with even moisture through the growing season.

planting.note: Replant divisions in early fall or early spring into rich, evenly moist soil.

directions: Bred by Marty Schafer and Jan Sacks of Joe Pye Weed's Garden, this glowing yellow Siberian iris reflects their long push to deepen and brighten the yellow tones available in the species beyond the pale tints of earlier cultivars. It brings strong color to the early-summer border and pairs well with blue and violet Siberian iris selections. Grow in full sun to light shade with consistent moisture.

planting.note: Divide and replant in early fall or early spring to maintain vigorous flowering clumps.

directions: Hybridized by Marty Schafer and Jan Sacks of Joe Pye Weed's Garden, this Siberian iris has golden falls netted and veined in purple, an unusual patterned effect that sets it apart from solid-colored selections. The contrast is especially striking massed in groups. Grow in full sun to light shade with even moisture and divide every few years as clumps thicken.
